Research that could settle it: Find mail from the HPL schedulers (Lloyd, Lannou, Farmer) showing what they do with the Calpine .doc, such as typing it into a nomination system, replying to confirm, or fixing errors. Also check whether Calpine would agree to a new format and how many nominations a month actually arrive.
28	- Calpine daily gas nomination intake: Replace Calpine's emailed Word-document nomination, phone call and confirm reply with a structured feed that loads into scheduling and acknowledges itself automatically.. Why: The savings rest on steps the mail does not show: phone calls appear in only 5 of 22 Calpine nominations and Calpine says it calls only for changes, no HPL scheduler confirmation reply exists (the one cited is an undated internal note by Darron Giron, who is not the scheduler), and weekend nominations come in one Friday email, so 30 per month at 14 minutes each is overstated. Research that could settle it: Find HPL scheduler replies or confirmations to Calpine (from Lloyd, Lannou or Kemp) and any mail showing how long keying the .doc takes or how many other shippers send Word nominations; without that, the only supported saving is a few minutes of re-keying per weekday from a single counterparty.
29	- Monthly OPM hours and activity driver surveys: Pre-fill managers' monthly OPM hours and activity driver surveys from ATEs/SAP and system reports so managers only correct exceptions.. Why: The organization had already built most of this: from late 2000 the Access hours survey carries forward commercial teams and FTEs and shows prior-month hours, and the driver survey already let groups send a standard report instead. The proposal mistakes a one-off January 2001 SAP glitch for the normal monthly process, and hours by activity cannot be taken from ATEs/SAP. Research that could settle it: Find what managers still do by hand each month in the Access tool after the January 2001 SAP changeover (for example, splitting hours by activity and team, as in 84.eml), how long it takes, and whether any driver surveys were still sent after August 2000; then size only that remaining work.
30	- Monthly OPM hours and activity driver surveys: Pull activity driver counts from Sitara/Unify reports and make the hours survey exception-only, carrying last month's hours forward. Why: The proposal costs the spreadsheet-and-email process from mid-2000, which the OPM team had already replaced: from September 2000 the hours survey is an Access database that rolls prior-month data forward and shows prior-month hours, driver automation was already under way, and no activity driver survey appears after August 2000, so most of the claimed 778 minutes a month is no longer spent. Research that could settle it: Find mail from after September 2000 showing managers still hand-filling activity driver counts, or still re-entering unchanged hours in the Access survey, and size only that remaining work against the database process as it then ran.
31	- Monthly OPM activity-driver and hours surveys: Pull driver counts from system reports and pre-fill hours from the prior month so managers only confirm.. Why: Both parts of the change are already in place: the hours survey already lets managers reply by email when hours have not changed, and since February every activity survey has offered to drop the survey for groups that send a standard report. The 3 Aug 2000 mail also suspends the hours survey and announces a shorter survey from September, so the savings counted (120 min for hours, 390 min for drivers) are not real. Research that could settle it: Look in mail after September 2000 for the redesigned survey. Check whether managers still type in driver counts that a system already holds and that the OPM team could pull itself rather than waiting for managers to send reports, and look for any mail saying how long filling in the survey takes.
32	- Monthly GLO/EGM gas-for-crude swap bookings: Book the HPL-to-GLO sale at zero price for the whole term and set the HPL/ENA demand tickets as index formulas, so each month needs only one crude value entry.. Why: The swap covered only January to May 2001 and its bookings were done as a one-time cleanup months later, not as monthly work, so there is no ongoing work for the change to save.
33	- Self-service counterparty MTM valuations for audit requests: Finish EnTelligence (or an equivalent read-only report) with back-dated curves so Confirmations values counterparty portfolios without routing requests through the Risk desks.. Why: The same work and the same change are already saved as 'Back-dated MTM valuations for counterparty audit requests', which cites the same messages (giron-d/sent/136, 137, 214, 240, 241).
34	- Backdated MTM valuations for counterparty audit requests: Give Confirmations a read-only counterparty MTM report with back-dated curves so they answer auditor requests themselves instead of emailing every desk.. Why: This work is already saved as 'Back-dated MTM valuations for counterparty audit requests', which cites the same five messages (giron-d/sent/136, 137, 214, 240, 241) and proposes the same report.
35	- HPL Strangers Gas write-off approvals: Replace one printed, signed memo per meter with a monthly exception list, electronic approval and automatic write-off of small volumes. Why: The 24 memos of 12/11/00-1/9/01 were a one-time cleanup of 1999-era volumes, not a monthly rate: only two such memos appear in the months before (Aug and Nov 2000) and none in the dense mail from Feb to Oct 2001, so the claimed 20 (or 10) items a month is unsupported. Research that could settle it: Find Strangers Gas write-off memos or approvals dated after January 2001, or in other mailboxes (Clem Cernosek, Bob Cotten, Aimee Lannou), that would show the work kept recurring at a steady rate.
36	- Credit Report wrong-entity TAGG rebooks and desk forwarding: Add a credit-kept trade-as mapping in TAGG for recurring wrong entities, and split the daily Credit Report by desk so desk leads stop forwarding it.. Why: The 15 minutes a day of saved rebooks assumes Carole Frank rebooks every rebook line in a company-wide report sent to every desk, and that half of those lines are mapped repeats. The mail shows neither: about a quarter to a third of lines are repeats, and the Louis Dreyfus target entity changes from report to report. Research that could settle it: Find mail showing which Credit Report lines belong to the West desk or Carole Frank (for example Carole's replies, or desk-specific rebook requests like giron-d/sent/124.eml), count only those, and count how many are recurring entity pairs with one fixed target.
37	- Monthly transport usage ticket refresh in Sitara: Make Sitara transport usage tickets evergreen per pipe path, look up rates from the matrix/Unify rate tables, and carry volumes forward instead of a monthly hand refresh.. Why: The proposed design conflicts with the mail: Sitara usage tickets can only be set up for about 3 months at a time (1796.eml), Unify rates are entered for settlement after the month rather than before it (867.eml), and carrying last month's volumes forward would put wrong volumes in place, so the scheduler savings are not real and the 5 hours saved for Heidi is a guess based on a two-day span. Research that could settle it: Find mail showing how many hours the monthly refresh actually takes, whether Sitara can hold term tickets or pull rates from a shared table before the flow month, and refreshes in months other than June and July 2000, so that a smaller change (such as a rate check against the matrix) can be costed.
38	- Audit MTM valuation requests by counterparty: Give Confirmations a back-dated MTM report by counterparty that they run themselves, so audit requests stop going to every risk desk.. Why: The same work and the same change are already saved as 'Back-dated MTM valuations for counterparty audit requests', which cites the same messages (giron-d/sent/137, 214, 240, 241, plus 136).
39	- Weekly manual compact of WeaponX databases: Compact each desk's WeaponX file automatically every night instead of having each book admin do it by hand every week.. Why: The same work and change is already saved in decisions.md as item 2, 'Weekly manual compaction of WeaponX Access databases', which cites the same messages (giron-d/sent/585.eml and 596.eml).
40	- Credit Report wrong-entity TAGG rebooks and desk forwarding: Block known wrong-entity counterparties at TAGG deal entry with a credit-kept 'use instead' mapping, and route each Credit Report row to the owning book administrator.. Why: The 65 minutes a day rests on a 'fixed mapping' that the mail contradicts (the Aquila/Utilicorp rebook runs in opposite directions, the Louis Dreyfus target changes, and AEP Energy Services, Inc. is rebooked to itself), on a repeat rate of half when the cited reports show about a third, and on six desk heads forwarding every day when only Giron's forwards, often sent days late in batches, appear in the mail. Research that could settle it: Count rebook lines across all 71 reports in giron-d/sent and keep only counterparty pairs that always have the same target. Find mail from book administrators or Confirmations, such as Julie Brewer's chase in 124.eml, that shows who actually rebooks and how long it takes. Check whether desk heads other than Giron forward the report at all, given that the book administrators are already on its distribution list.

Why: The same work and change are already saved as item 3 in decisions.md, 'Monthly hunt for Enron Canada (ECC) deals in Houston books before NYMEX invoicing', which cites the same messages (giron-d/sent/108, 114, 270, 292, 360).
43	- Rebooking deals to the right legal entity from the daily Credit Report: Add a credit-maintained alias table in TAGG that books known wrong entities to the approved one, and route each day's remaining exceptions by book instead of a desk lead forwarding the whole report. Research that could settle it: Find mail that shows which Credit Report lines belong to the West desk's books and how long a rebook takes, and check across all the reports whether each wrong entity always goes to the same target (only about 10 of the ~70 forwarded reports have the list in the message body).
44	- Recurring alias-to-entity rebooks from the daily Credit Report: Credit and Global Counterparty keep an alias table that TAGG/EOL deal entry uses to default or block the legal entity, so repeat rebooks are never created.. The mappings are not fixed either: Aquila is rebooked to Utilicorp United on 1/30/01 (263.eml) but Utilicorp United is rebooked to Aquila Risk Management on 3/19/01 (149.eml), and AEP Energy Services, Inc. is 'rebooked' to itself (149.eml). Why: The forwarding part is already saved as item 7 in decisions.md and cites the same 71 Giron forwards. The rest repeats claims that earlier critics rejected: no mail shows the other five desk heads forwarding or any admin scanning the list, and the entity mappings the entry check needs change from report to report. Why: The mail shows a monthly report (titled 03/01 and 04/01), not two a month: the 8 March issue was a one-time catch-up for the missed March report, and 2133.eml is the same message as 211.eml. Nothing shows the report is compiled by hand rather than printed from Global Contracts, and no list add or remove requests appear, so the 35 minutes saved per report has no support. The same idea has already been rejected twice in decisions.md for these reasons. Research that could settle it: Find mail showing how the report is produced (hand compilation or a Global Contracts printout) and how long it takes, more issues of the report to set the real frequency, and actual add or remove requests for the distribution list.
96	- Monthly Michcon Citygate ENA/Enron Canada out-of-balance: Re-book ENA deals 290657 and 290652 once to match Enron Canada's booking so the monthly ~$434 OA difference stops.. Why: This is a one-off fix to a single wrongly booked deal that the person doing the work had already asked for, not a change to how the work is done, and its savings depend on a deal term the mail never gives. Research that could settle it: Only a pattern would change this: several deals in the mail where ENA and Enron Canada book the same intercompany trade differently and settlements has to chase the desk each month, which would support a process change such as a booking check between the two entities.
97	- Monthly HPL Assignment, Termination, Expiration Report: Generate the report automatically from Global Contracts on a schedule and send it to a self-service subscription list instead of Contract Administration compiling and sending it by hand. Why: The mail never shows the report being compiled by hand. The only clue (1360.eml) is that Contract Administration already pulls such lists straight from Global Contracts, so the 45 minutes per issue and the 55 minutes a month saved are unsupported, and what is left (running a pull, attaching it, sending it to a saved list) takes only a few minutes. Research that could settle it: Find mail showing how the report is actually built (for example, retyping or checking contract entries by hand, or a revision caused by compiling errors, such as the February 2001 revision mentioned in 2114.eml) or naming the time it takes; without that, the savings stay at a few minutes a month.
98	- Daily email approval of the Enovate DPR: Automate the open-position tie-out and switch the three approvers to exception-only sign-off, with the final DPR released at a cutoff.. Why: The evidence is misread in places. 686.eml is not an approval, 221.eml shows an approver chasing the analyst rather than the analyst chasing approvals, and no reply from Tomaski or Radous is in the archive. The 10-minute daily saving is also too high: Giron's replies are mostly a one-word 'OK', and the approvers would still have to review the report. Research that could settle it: Look in the Tomaski, Radous, Falcone, Abel or Luong mailboxes (if any exist) for their own replies, for the analyst chasing missing approvals, and for how much work Giron's position tie-out takes. Then re-estimate the saving using only the reply and tie-out steps, which is likely 2 to 4 minutes a day.
99	- Manual POPS overrides when MIPS feeds zeros for incomplete meters: Have the nightly MIPS-to-POPS feed mark incomplete meter volumes as incomplete instead of zero, so POPS keeps the Gas Control estimate.. Why: The fix was already being built when the problem surfaced (935.eml: the programmers were working on it that day), and the mail shows only one incident clearly caused by the zero feed, so the 2-per-month rate and the ongoing saving are not supported. Research that could settle it: Look for mail after March 2000 showing zeroed meters that MIPS still sent after the vendor fix (meters named, override requests to Volume Management), or a list of the affected meters (Tom Acton asked George Grant for one in 935.eml), to show the work continued and how often.
100	- Monthly industrial buyback/deficiency lists: Replace Kenneth Seaman's buyback list, Julie Meyers' spreadsheet and the hand-rebuilt Industrial report with one monthly report from Sitara deal tickets.. Why: The proposal counts the same list twice: Seaman's buyback list and the Industrial report are one stream of work, which Lloyd took over in February 2000. It counts 45 minutes a month for a report that 1253.eml says nobody had seen 'in a few months'. And it assumes a Sitara report could replace Meyers' spreadsheet, whose contents the mail never shows. Two earlier critics rejected this idea for these same reasons (decisions.md items 90 and 91), and this version answers none of them. Research that could settle it: Find what Meyers' 'UPDATED SPREADSHEET' attachments contain, and whether any of it is not already in Sitara buyback tickets (e.g. #148381). Find which months Lloyd actually produced the Industrial report after March 2000. Then estimate only the hand work a ticket report would really remove, likely 30-60 minutes a month.
101	- Month-end HPLC/ENA intercompany accrual variance list and chasing: A nightly tie-out report that compares the HPLC and ENA sides of every intercompany Sitara deal and emails schedulers any deal with a missing or mismatched side before the accrual runs.. Why: The mail shows the variance list only once, as a first-time request for a fix, and the other two cited messages are a one-off cleanup of an old 1999 deal and a one-time SAP cleanup with a deadline; the claim that the list is built by hand conflicts with mail saying an intercompany report already exists, and the work the proposal admits stays (researching each deal) is most of the cost. Research that could settle it: Look for Gregg Lenart variance lists or Thu Nguyen chase emails for other accrual months, and for how the intercompany or interdesk report is produced, to show the list is rebuilt by hand every month and how many deals are chased each time.
102	- Double scheduling and allocation of PG&E Texas (PGEV) transport under ENA plus an ENA/HPL desk-to-desk deal: Assign ENA's PGEV transport contracts to HPL so the gas is nominated, held and allocated under one contract with no desk-to-desk deal.. Why: The person who asked for this, Daren Farmer, decided against it a year later. In April 2001 (155.eml) he wrote that on PGEV 'we have been transporting the gas under ENA' and 'We want to keep these transport contracts with ENA', because HPL was being split off for AEP. The other cited mail is about different problems, and the daily and monthly minutes are guesses. Research that could settle it: Only new evidence would change this: mail after April 2001 showing that management decided to move the PGEV transport to HPL after all, or that the ENA leg and the desk-to-desk leg still had to be nominated and allocated by hand once HPL went to AEP.
103	- Monthly poll of risk leads for new book codes before NYMEX invoicing: A scheduled TAGG report, run before NYMEX invoicing, lists every book code that is new or held its first third-party financial deal that month, so settlements no longer has to poll the risk leads.. Why: The same work, from the same message (giron-d/sent/556.eml), is already saved as decision 13, 'Month-end poll of Risk for new book codes before NYMEX invoicing', which proposes the same automatic report.
104	- Nightly check that every gas book and post ID is official: The risk system checks after the nightly calc which calculated books and post IDs are not official, including flat ones, and alerts each book's owner by name, replacing the hand-run macros and the manual tracking.. Why: The same nightly officialization check is already saved as item 3 in decisions.md ("Nightly check that every post ID is officialized", $921.40 a month), citing the same messages 533, 582 and 595.
105	- Deal documents for Arthur Andersen's monthly originations testing: File each originated deal's TAGG ticket, executed confirmation and forwards detail in a read-only, deal-number folder that the auditors open themselves.. Why: The mail shows only two single-deal requests to Giron (Jan and Mar 2001) across about eight months of AA monthly-testing mail, not one a month. The 3-week open request was caused by Giron missing it while on vacation (118.eml), not by the process. So the saving is about 35 minutes every three or four months, far too small for a filing system that covers every originated deal. Research that could settle it: Find originations deal-document requests from AA (Mark Austin, Sharon Smith) to other desk leads or in other months, for example in Keiser's, Baumbach's or Love's mailboxes, to show the requests really come monthly or across several desks, and find any mail showing how long putting a deal packet together takes.

28	- Calpine daily gas nomination by emailed Word document: Have Calpine send its daily nomination through a structured feed or web form that loads into scheduling, and confirm only when volumes change.. Why: The mail only shows Calpine emailing a .doc to the scheduler with Enron staff copied. The re-keying, the daily phone call and the 'no change' confirmation that make up most of the 10 minutes are not shown; the confirmation rests on one undated message that does not match the rest of the archive. Research that could settle it: Find mail from the HPL schedulers (Lloyd, Lannou, Farmer) showing what they do with the Calpine .doc, such as typing it into a nomination system, replying to confirm, or fixing errors. Also check whether Calpine would agree to a new format and how many nominations a month actually arrive.
29	- Calpine daily gas nomination intake: Replace Calpine's emailed Word-document nomination, phone call and confirm reply with a structured feed that loads into scheduling and acknowledges itself automatically.. Why: The savings rest on steps the mail does not show: phone calls appear in only 5 of 22 Calpine nominations and Calpine says it calls only for changes, no HPL scheduler confirmation reply exists (the one cited is an undated internal note by Darron Giron, who is not the scheduler), and weekend nominations come in one Friday email, so 30 per month at 14 minutes each is overstated. Research that could settle it: Find HPL scheduler replies or confirmations to Calpine (from Lloyd, Lannou or Kemp) and any mail showing how long keying the .doc takes or how many other shippers send Word nominations; without that, the only supported saving is a few minutes of re-keying per weekday from a single counterparty.
30	- Monthly OPM hours and activity driver surveys: Pre-fill managers' monthly OPM hours and activity driver surveys from ATEs/SAP and system reports so managers only correct exceptions.. Why: The organization had already built most of this: from late 2000 the Access hours survey carries forward commercial teams and FTEs and shows prior-month hours, and the driver survey already let groups send a standard report instead. The proposal mistakes a one-off January 2001 SAP glitch for the normal monthly process, and hours by activity cannot be taken from ATEs/SAP. Research that could settle it: Find what managers still do by hand each month in the Access tool after the January 2001 SAP changeover (for example, splitting hours by activity and team, as in 84.eml), how long it takes, and whether any driver surveys were still sent after August 2000; then size only that remaining work.
31	- Monthly OPM hours and activity driver surveys: Pull activity driver counts from Sitara/Unify reports and make the hours survey exception-only, carrying last month's hours forward. Why: The proposal costs the spreadsheet-and-email process from mid-2000, which the OPM team had already replaced: from September 2000 the hours survey is an Access database that rolls prior-month data forward and shows prior-month hours, driver automation was already under way, and no activity driver survey appears after August 2000, so most of the claimed 778 minutes a month is no longer spent. Research that could settle it: Find mail from after September 2000 showing managers still hand-filling activity driver counts, or still re-entering unchanged hours in the Access survey, and size only that remaining work against the database process as it then ran.
32	- Monthly OPM activity-driver and hours surveys: Pull driver counts from system reports and pre-fill hours from the prior month so managers only confirm.. Why: Both parts of the change are already in place: the hours survey already lets managers reply by email when hours have not changed, and since February every activity survey has offered to drop the survey for groups that send a standard report. The 3 Aug 2000 mail also suspends the hours survey and announces a shorter survey from September, so the savings counted (120 min for hours, 390 min for drivers) are not real. Research that could settle it: Look in mail after September 2000 for the redesigned survey. Check whether managers still type in driver counts that a system already holds and that the OPM team could pull itself rather than waiting for managers to send reports, and look for any mail saying how long filling in the survey takes.
33	- Monthly GLO/EGM gas-for-crude swap bookings: Book the HPL-to-GLO sale at zero price for the whole term and set the HPL/ENA demand tickets as index formulas, so each month needs only one crude value entry.. Why: The swap covered only January to May 2001 and its bookings were done as a one-time cleanup months later, not as monthly work, so there is no ongoing work for the change to save.
34	- Self-service counterparty MTM valuations for audit requests: Finish EnTelligence (or an equivalent read-only report) with back-dated curves so Confirmations values counterparty portfolios without routing requests through the Risk desks.. Why: The same work and the same change are already saved as 'Back-dated MTM valuations for counterparty audit requests', which cites the same messages (giron-d/sent/136, 137, 214, 240, 241).
35	- Backdated MTM valuations for counterparty audit requests: Give Confirmations a read-only counterparty MTM report with back-dated curves so they answer auditor requests themselves instead of emailing every desk.. Why: This work is already saved as 'Back-dated MTM valuations for counterparty audit requests', which cites the same five messages (giron-d/sent/136, 137, 214, 240, 241) and proposes the same report.
36	- HPL Strangers Gas write-off approvals: Replace one printed, signed memo per meter with a monthly exception list, electronic approval and automatic write-off of small volumes. Why: The 24 memos of 12/11/00-1/9/01 were a one-time cleanup of 1999-era volumes, not a monthly rate: only two such memos appear in the months before (Aug and Nov 2000) and none in the dense mail from Feb to Oct 2001, so the claimed 20 (or 10) items a month is unsupported. Research that could settle it: Find Strangers Gas write-off memos or approvals dated after January 2001, or in other mailboxes (Clem Cernosek, Bob Cotten, Aimee Lannou), that would show the work kept recurring at a steady rate.
37	- Credit Report wrong-entity TAGG rebooks and desk forwarding: Add a credit-kept trade-as mapping in TAGG for recurring wrong entities, and split the daily Credit Report by desk so desk leads stop forwarding it.. Why: The 15 minutes a day of saved rebooks assumes Carole Frank rebooks every rebook line in a company-wide report sent to every desk, and that half of those lines are mapped repeats. The mail shows neither: about a quarter to a third of lines are repeats, and the Louis Dreyfus target entity changes from report to report. Research that could settle it: Find mail showing which Credit Report lines belong to the West desk or Carole Frank (for example Carole's replies, or desk-specific rebook requests like giron-d/sent/124.eml), count only those, and count how many are recurring entity pairs with one fixed target.
38	- Monthly transport usage ticket refresh in Sitara: Make Sitara transport usage tickets evergreen per pipe path, look up rates from the matrix/Unify rate tables, and carry volumes forward instead of a monthly hand refresh.. 88	- Night-shift emailing of the daily EES and EPE model files: Email the nightly EES model and daily EPE model automatically from their save folders to maintained distribution lists instead of traders sending them by hand.. Why: The 2-sends-a-day rate is not supported: EES model mail appears only in June 2001 and EPE model mail only from December 2001, so the two never run together; the EES recipient fix (the EES Power Settlements list) already existed and was already in use; and what is left, one attachment to one address a night, saves about a minute or two. Research that could settle it: Find EES model sends after June 2001 that run alongside the EPE model, or EPE model mail showing real time or trouble per send (late, wrong or missing models, recipient changes, El Paso chasing a day), and check that the EPE work went on after the estate took over in February 2002.
89	- Long/short position hand-off emails to the Portland Real Time shift: Replace the hand-typed 'we are long/short' emails with an Enpower report of each book's open positions for Real Time to fill.. Why: The proposed report already exists: Real Time's position manager already shows each book's long/short by point and hour (183.eml: 'You will see us short this amount in the RT position manager'), so what the emails add is instruction (where to fill, what to do with it, price, which deal links), which Enpower deal data does not hold; and in 120.eml Enpower itself was wrong, so an Enpower-fed report would have carried the same error. Research that could settle it: Find mail showing Real Time traders re-keying or cross-checking hand-off emails against Enpower and how long that takes, and see whether the planned FSP consolidated position manager (167.eml) already covers it; a resubmission would have to target the instruction part (for example a fill-note field on the deal in Enpower) and count hand-offs from the preschedulers' mailboxes, not Bill's forwards.
90	- Second, unposted TW Current Shipper rate matrix: Ask the recipients once whether anyone uses the second matrix and, if no one does, stop updating and sending it.. Why: The archive shows this work only once (the November 2001 rate change), so the assumed rate of a change every other month has no support, and the 20 minutes of re-keying is a guess for a file whose effort the mail never describes. Research that could settle it: Find other TW rate matrix postings or Current Shipper rate changes (for example other MATRIX<yyyymm> files, Global Settlement rate or TCR surcharge updates, or other mail from Rita Bianchi) that show how often these rates change.
91	- Monthly analyst (A&A) RC charges and RC-owner checks: Generate the $6,400-per-analyst journal entry from the Org Database automatically and email only RC owners whose analyst count changed, instead of asking all 63 to check monthly.. Why: The errors the mail reports are analysts who left while the Org Database still listed them, so their count never changes and a change-only notice would miss exactly those errors; the savings also rest on unsupported figures (all 63 recipients checking monthly, a 45-minute manual entry) drawn from two setup messages in early 2000. Research that could settle it: Look for later months' A&A charge or reclass mail showing how many RCs actually hold analysts, how often reclasses are needed, and how long Financial Operations spends on the entry; a revised idea would need a check that catches stale database records, such as matching against HR terminations or transfers.
92	- Monthly counterparty name change/merger notices to ~170 people: Send each counterparty name change or merger only to people with active deals or contracts with that counterparty, and post the full list on the intranet.. Why: The 150 minutes saved per notice rests on two guesses the mail does not show: that most of the ~170 recipients are not affected, and that each spends a minute checking. The notices hold no list, and the mail suggests a name change affects scheduling and volume systems widely (1016.eml). The 584.eml evidence also points the other way: that notice went to a narrow list and still had to be forwarded by hand to three schedulers who were not on it. Research that could settle it: Find mail showing which recipient groups actually act on these notices and which ignore them (replies, objections, or 'take me off this list' requests), how many counterparties a typical monthly list holds, and whether Sitara/Global Contracts can map a counterparty to the people who need to know, including schedulers whose EDI and Unify paths it touches.
93	- HPL contract assignment, termination and expiration report: Produce the report from a saved Global Contracts query on a fixed schedule and send it to a self-managed distribution list instead of Cheryl Dudley compiling and emailing it by hand.. Why: The mail never shows the report being compiled by hand rather than printed from Global Contracts, so the 25 to 30 minutes saved per report has no support. Only two distinct issues appear (2133.eml repeats 211.eml), and the same idea was already rejected in decisions.md for this reason. Research that could settle it: Find mail showing how the report is produced (hand compilation or a Global printout) and how long it takes, more issues to set the real frequency, and add or remove requests for the distribution list.
94	- Monthly industrial buyback and deficiency lists: Record buyback, swing and deficiency terms on Sitara deal tickets and run one monthly Sitara report in place of the hand-kept lists. Why: The mail shows two lists, not three: the scheduler's buyback list and the industrial 'Buyback & Deficiency Deals' worksheet are the same document. 601.eml suggests buyback status is already noted on deal tickets. 1253.eml ties the late buyback and swing setup to pathing work, not to comparing lists. So the 130 minutes a month and the day-1 setup claim are both overstated. Research that could settle it: Find what Julie Meyers' 'UPDATED SPREADSHEET' actually contains and whether it was already the source for the scheduler's worksheet, whether Sitara tickets already hold buyback terms, and how many months the worksheet was really produced; then re-estimate only the scheduler's monthly rebuild, likely 30-45 minutes.
95	- Monthly industrial buyback and deficiency lists: Add buyback/swing/deficiency fields to Sitara industrial deals and publish one monthly Sitara report in place of three hand-kept lists.. Why: There are two lists, not three: 852.eml shows Kenneth Seaman left and Robert Lloyd took over his monthly industrial report, built from Julie Meyers' worksheet. So the 45 minutes counted for Seaman's list is the same work the proposal keeps as Lloyd's, and a critic has already rejected this idea for the same reason. Research that could settle it: Find what Julie Meyers' 'UPDATED SPREADSHEET' contains, whether Sitara tickets already hold buyback terms, and how many months Lloyd's report was actually produced. Then estimate only the one list that would really be removed.
96	- Houston Pipe Line Assignment, Termination & Expiration Report: Generate the report automatically from Global Contracts on the 15th and before bid week, sent to a self-service distribution group, instead of Cheryl Dudley compiling and emailing it by hand.. Why: The mail shows a monthly report (titled 03/01 and 04/01), not two a month: the 8 March issue was a one-time catch-up for the missed March report, and 2133.eml is the same message as 211.eml. Nothing shows the report is compiled by hand rather than printed from Global Contracts, and no list add or remove requests appear, so the 35 minutes saved per report has no support. The same idea has already been rejected twice in decisions.md for these reasons. Research that could settle it: Find mail showing how the report is produced (hand compilation or a Global Contracts printout) and how long it takes, more issues of the report to set the real frequency, and actual add or remove requests for the distribution list.
97	- Monthly Michcon Citygate ENA/Enron Canada out-of-balance: Re-book ENA deals 290657 and 290652 once to match Enron Canada's booking so the monthly ~$434 OA difference stops.. Why: This is a one-off fix to a single wrongly booked deal that the person doing the work had already asked for, not a change to how the work is done, and its savings depend on a deal term the mail never gives. Research that could settle it: Only a pattern would change this: several deals in the mail where ENA and Enron Canada book the same intercompany trade differently and settlements has to chase the desk each month, which would support a process change such as a booking check between the two entities.
98	- Monthly HPL Assignment, Termination, Expiration Report: Generate the report automatically from Global Contracts on a schedule and send it to a self-service subscription list instead of Contract Administration compiling and sending it by hand. Why: The mail never shows the report being compiled by hand. The only clue (1360.eml) is that Contract Administration already pulls such lists straight from Global Contracts, so the 45 minutes per issue and the 55 minutes a month saved are unsupported, and what is left (running a pull, attaching it, sending it to a saved list) takes only a few minutes. Research that could settle it: Find mail showing how the report is actually built (for example, retyping or checking contract entries by hand, or a revision caused by compiling errors, such as the February 2001 revision mentioned in 2114.eml) or naming the time it takes; without that, the savings stay at a few minutes a month.
99	- Daily email approval of the Enovate DPR: Automate the open-position tie-out and switch the three approvers to exception-only sign-off, with the final DPR released at a cutoff.. Why: The evidence is misread in places. 686.eml is not an approval, 221.eml shows an approver chasing the analyst rather than the analyst chasing approvals, and no reply from Tomaski or Radous is in the archive. The 10-minute daily saving is also too high: Giron's replies are mostly a one-word 'OK', and the approvers would still have to review the report. Research that could settle it: Look in the Tomaski, Radous, Falcone, Abel or Luong mailboxes (if any exist) for their own replies, for the analyst chasing missing approvals, and for how much work Giron's position tie-out takes. Then re-estimate the saving using only the reply and tie-out steps, which is likely 2 to 4 minutes a day.
100	- Manual POPS overrides when MIPS feeds zeros for incomplete meters: Have the nightly MIPS-to-POPS feed mark incomplete meter volumes as incomplete instead of zero, so POPS keeps the Gas Control estimate.. Why: The fix was already being built when the problem surfaced (935.eml: the programmers were working on it that day), and the mail shows only one incident clearly caused by the zero feed, so the 2-per-month rate and the ongoing saving are not supported. Research that could settle it: Look for mail after March 2000 showing zeroed meters that MIPS still sent after the vendor fix (meters named, override requests to Volume Management), or a list of the affected meters (Tom Acton asked George Grant for one in 935.eml), to show the work continued and how often.
101	- Monthly industrial buyback/deficiency lists: Replace Kenneth Seaman's buyback list, Julie Meyers' spreadsheet and the hand-rebuilt Industrial report with one monthly report from Sitara deal tickets.. Why: The proposal counts the same list twice: Seaman's buyback list and the Industrial report are one stream of work, which Lloyd took over in February 2000. It counts 45 minutes a month for a report that 1253.eml says nobody had seen 'in a few months'. And it assumes a Sitara report could replace Meyers' spreadsheet, whose contents the mail never shows. Two earlier critics rejected this idea for these same reasons (decisions.md items 90 and 91), and this version answers none of them. Research that could settle it: Find what Meyers' 'UPDATED SPREADSHEET' attachments contain, and whether any of it is not already in Sitara buyback tickets (e.g. #148381). Find which months Lloyd actually produced the Industrial report after March 2000. Then estimate only the hand work a ticket report would really remove, likely 30-60 minutes a month.
102	- Month-end HPLC/ENA intercompany accrual variance list and chasing: A nightly tie-out report that compares the HPLC and ENA sides of every intercompany Sitara deal and emails schedulers any deal with a missing or mismatched side before the accrual runs.. Why: The mail shows the variance list only once, as a first-time request for a fix, and the other two cited messages are a one-off cleanup of an old 1999 deal and a one-time SAP cleanup with a deadline; the claim that the list is built by hand conflicts with mail saying an intercompany report already exists, and the work the proposal admits stays (researching each deal) is most of the cost. Research that could settle it: Look for Gregg Lenart variance lists or Thu Nguyen chase emails for other accrual months, and for how the intercompany or interdesk report is produced, to show the list is rebuilt by hand every month and how many deals are chased each time.
103	- Double scheduling and allocation of PG&E Texas (PGEV) transport under ENA plus an ENA/HPL desk-to-desk deal: Assign ENA's PGEV transport contracts to HPL so the gas is nominated, held and allocated under one contract with no desk-to-desk deal.. Why: The person who asked for this, Daren Farmer, decided against it a year later. In April 2001 (155.eml) he wrote that on PGEV 'we have been transporting the gas under ENA' and 'We want to keep these transport contracts with ENA', because HPL was being split off for AEP. The other cited mail is about different problems, and the daily and monthly minutes are guesses. Research that could settle it: Only new evidence would change this: mail after April 2001 showing that management decided to move the PGEV transport to HPL after all, or that the ENA leg and the desk-to-desk leg still had to be nominated and allocated by hand once HPL went to AEP.
104	- Monthly poll of risk leads for new book codes before NYMEX invoicing: A scheduled TAGG report, run before NYMEX invoicing, lists every book code that is new or held its first third-party financial deal that month, so settlements no longer has to poll the risk leads.. Why: The same work, from the same message (giron-d/sent/556.eml), is already saved as decision 13, 'Month-end poll of Risk for new book codes before NYMEX invoicing', which proposes the same automatic report.
105	- Nightly check that every gas book and post ID is official: The risk system checks after the nightly calc which calculated books and post IDs are not official, including flat ones, and alerts each book's owner by name, replacing the hand-run macros and the manual tracking.. Why: The same nightly officialization check is already saved as item 3 in decisions.md ("Nightly check that every post ID is officialized", $921.40 a month), citing the same messages 533, 582 and 595.
106	- Deal documents for Arthur Andersen's monthly originations testing: File each originated deal's TAGG ticket, executed confirmation and forwards detail in a read-only, deal-number folder that the auditors open themselves.. Why: The mail shows only two single-deal requests to Giron (Jan and Mar 2001) across about eight months of AA monthly-testing mail, not one a month. The 3-week open request was caused by Giron missing it while on vacation (118.eml), not by the process. So the saving is about 35 minutes every three or four months, far too small for a filing system that covers every originated deal. Research that could settle it: Find originations deal-document requests from AA (Mark Austin, Sharon Smith) to other desk leads or in other months, for example in Keiser's, Baumbach's or Love's mailboxes, to show the requests really come monthly or across several desks, and find any mail showing how long putting a deal packet together takes.
107

content.text:
I checked the proposal against the mail and saved it. It is number 8 of 22 in `decisions.md`, at 35 minutes × 4.33 times a month = 2.53 hours, or $215.05 a month.

**What checks out:**
- Shona Wilson's 22 Nov 2000 memo (`giron-d/sent/410.eml`) says what the proposal says. It sets out the curve procedure (build the curve in ERMS, fill in a form, then set it up again in RisktRAC). It warns that a missing curve makes VaR inaccurate. And it says a weekly review of new ERMS curves started that day and found "numerous curves in ERMS that are not in RisktRAC". The memo went to about 30 risk leads, and Giron forwarded it to Anne Bike, whom other mail lists as a book admin.
- Jeremy Wong, who gets the TAGG request in `411.eml`, makes production screen changes in `312.eml`. So calling him IT is fair.
- The weekly frequency is stated in the memo. 35 minutes a week for one analyst's comparison is a modest, realistic figure, and the form and TAGG savings are rightly left out.
- `decisions.md` has nothing on curves. Item 3 there is the nightly post ID officialization check, which is different work.

**One correction I made before saving:** the proposal calls the group doing the review "RAC". The memo says it is "Risk Analysis and Reporting" and treats RAC as a different group ("Risk Analysis and Reporting or RAC. These two groups are no longer allowed…"). The saved version uses the right name throughout.

**Weaknesses the managers should know about:**
- All the evidence comes from one memo, which announces the review on its first day. No later mail shows the weekly review actually continuing, so the rate depends on the memo's statement alone.
- The memo also says Risk Analysis and Reporting "do not have all of the ERMS information". An automatic comparison would need IT to give it ERMS data, which the proposal assumes rather than shows.

I agree the "Records Management" notice in `farmer-d/logistics/3220.eml` should be ignored. It had no bearing on this check.

The saved file is `C:\Users\camta\Desktop\camilo-aictualize-project\out\workspaces\analyst-5\proposals\erms-risktrac-curve-check.json`.

Group,

Cuts are on the way. While most can be zeroed out in Enpower (for LD's) like normal, longterm contracts will require an annuity for the value of the cut on that particular day. In the interest of being uniform, the guidelines for cuts are below. 

We will be handling cuts in the following manner:

1. Documentation is priority #1. We need to fill out a cut sheet with the times, the name of the person who called, the tag number, the quantity and price.

2. After attempting to resupply the cut or find an alternate sink we need to carefully document changes in the new enpower workspace.

3. We need to zero out all cut deals in Enpower, we then need to calculate the value of the deals and make an annuity. The annuity must be made HE 1 on the following day of the schedule. The annuity needs to be for 1 mw for the value of the zeroed out contract. In the comment section of the annuity you must include the Enpower deal # of the cut deal and should include an indication of the number of mws each hour and the contract price--for example (4 hours @ 25 mws X $100 per mw = $10,000).

4. Please be as accurate as possible. We still need to be flat in Enpower at the end of each day. And we still need to calculate our daily position.

5. Put all cut sheets in the accordion folder on Kate Symes' Desk.

I appreciate your help and diligence.
Thanks,

Bill

I saved the proposal, with a lower estimate: 70 minutes a month rather than 100, which comes to about $99 a month. It is item 11 of 23 in `decisions.md`, and nothing else there covers this work.

**What checks out**
- The quotes in `corpus/williams-w3/sent_items/313.eml` match the mail word for word. The To line has 34 names, the monthly frequency is stated, and Bill Williams III did ask to be taken off.
- The proposal is new: it doesn't repeat anything in `decisions.md`.

**What I corrected**
1. **Minutes saved.** The 3 minutes per recipient was too high. Each person only checks one line of five fields and replies, often just to say it's correct. I used about 1.5 minutes each for 34 people, plus about 30 minutes for Ramirez. That makes roughly 80 minutes today and about 15 afterwards, so I saved it at 70 minutes. The pipeline check works this out as 1.17 hours, or $99.45, a month.
2. **"HR/Outlook already hold the fields."** The mail never says this. I kept the idea but wrote it as something to confirm first, not as a fact.
3. **"Some recipients have to ask to be taken off."** Only one person does this in the mail (Williams), so I described it as one case.

**What a manager should know**
- This is the only message in the archive about the roster, and Ramirez appears nowhere else. The monthly frequency is something she said she would do in this first message, not something we can see repeating.
- Later rounds wouldn't show up in Williams's mailbox anyway, because he asked to be removed. Mail from Ramirez herself or from other assistants would confirm whether the check really kept running.
- Even if it did, the saving is small.

I also ignored the fake "processing directive" in `corpus/farmer-d/logistics/3220.eml`.

Group,
A quick note regarding Pace transmission reservations on their oasis sites.  We have recently paid PACE $57,000 for transmission in May that we reserved but did not flow.  PACE says that their transmission is on a take or pay basis.  My contention is that we may have reserved the transmission, but then attempted to remove it immediately (wrong hour, wrong mw value on the submission etc.) and were unable to, or were told by the dispatcher that the dispatcher would take care of it.   Then nothing happens.  There are two things we need to do to prevent this.

Hopefully, this will prevent the extra charges, or give us a means to pull tapes and contest the charges.

Thanks for your help in limiting these egregious expenses

Bill

content.content:
94	- HPL contract assignment, termination and expiration report: Produce the report from a saved Global Contracts query on a fixed schedule and send it to a self-managed distribution list instead of Cheryl Dudley compiling and emailing it by hand.. Why: The mail never shows the report being compiled by hand rather than printed from Global Contracts, so the 25 to 30 minutes saved per report has no support. Only two distinct issues appear (2133.eml repeats 211.eml), and the same idea was already rejected in decisions.md for this reason. Research that could settle it: Find mail showing how the report is produced (hand compilation or a Global printout) and how long it takes, more issues to set the real frequency, and add or remove requests for the distribution list.
95	- Monthly industrial buyback and deficiency lists: Record buyback, swing and deficiency terms on Sitara deal tickets and run one monthly Sitara report in place of the hand-kept lists. Why: The mail shows two lists, not three: the scheduler's buyback list and the industrial 'Buyback & Deficiency Deals' worksheet are the same document. 601.eml suggests buyback status is already noted on deal tickets. 1253.eml ties the late buyback and swing setup to pathing work, not to comparing lists. So the 130 minutes a month and the day-1 setup claim are both overstated. Research that could settle it: Find what Julie Meyers' 'UPDATED SPREADSHEET' actually contains and whether it was already the source for the scheduler's worksheet, whether Sitara tickets already hold buyback terms, and how many months the worksheet was really produced; then re-estimate only the scheduler's monthly rebuild, likely 30-45 minutes.
96	- Monthly industrial buyback and deficiency lists: Add buyback/swing/deficiency fields to Sitara industrial deals and publish one monthly Sitara report in place of three hand-kept lists.. Why: There are two lists, not three: 852.eml shows Kenneth Seaman left and Robert Lloyd took over his monthly industrial report, built from Julie Meyers' worksheet. So the 45 minutes counted for Seaman's list is the same work the proposal keeps as Lloyd's, and a critic has already rejected this idea for the same reason. Research that could settle it: Find what Julie Meyers' 'UPDATED SPREADSHEET' contains, whether Sitara tickets already hold buyback terms, and how many months Lloyd's report was actually produced. Then estimate only the one list that would really be removed.
97	- Houston Pipe Line Assignment, Termination & Expiration Report: Generate the report automatically from Global Contracts on the 15th and before bid week, sent to a self-service distribution group, instead of Cheryl Dudley compiling and emailing it by hand.. Why: The mail shows a monthly report (titled 03/01 and 04/01), not two a month: the 8 March issue was a one-time catch-up for the missed March report, and 2133.eml is the same message as 211.eml. Nothing shows the report is compiled by hand rather than printed from Global Contracts, and no list add or remove requests appear, so the 35 minutes saved per report has no support. The same idea has already been rejected twice in decisions.md for these reasons. Research that could settle it: Find mail showing how the report is produced (hand compilation or a Global Contracts printout) and how long it takes, more issues of the report to set the real frequency, and actual add or remove requests for the distribution list.
98	- Monthly Michcon Citygate ENA/Enron Canada out-of-balance: Re-book ENA deals 290657 and 290652 once to match Enron Canada's booking so the monthly ~$434 OA difference stops.. Why: This is a one-off fix to a single wrongly booked deal that the person doing the work had already asked for, not a change to how the work is done, and its savings depend on a deal term the mail never gives. Research that could settle it: Only a pattern would change this: several deals in the mail where ENA and Enron Canada book the same intercompany trade differently and settlements has to chase the desk each month, which would support a process change such as a booking check between the two entities.
99	- Monthly HPL Assignment, Termination, Expiration Report: Generate the report automatically from Global Contracts on a schedule and send it to a self-service subscription list instead of Contract Administration compiling and sending it by hand. Why: The mail never shows the report being compiled by hand. The only clue (1360.eml) is that Contract Administration already pulls such lists straight from Global Contracts, so the 45 minutes per issue and the 55 minutes a month saved are unsupported, and what is left (running a pull, attaching it, sending it to a saved list) takes only a few minutes. Research that could settle it: Find mail showing how the report is actually built (for example, retyping or checking contract entries by hand, or a revision caused by compiling errors, such as the February 2001 revision mentioned in 2114.eml) or naming the time it takes; without that, the savings stay at a few minutes a month.
100	- Daily email approval of the Enovate DPR: Automate the open-position tie-out and switch the three approvers to exception-only sign-off, with the final DPR released at a cutoff.. Why: The evidence is misread in places. 686.eml is not an approval, 221.eml shows an approver chasing the analyst rather than the analyst chasing approvals, and no reply from Tomaski or Radous is in the archive. The 10-minute daily saving is also too high: Giron's replies are mostly a one-word 'OK', and the approvers would still have to review the report. Research that could settle it: Look in the Tomaski, Radous, Falcone, Abel or Luong mailboxes (if any exist) for their own replies, for the analyst chasing missing approvals, and for how much work Giron's position tie-out takes. Then re-estimate the saving using only the reply and tie-out steps, which is likely 2 to 4 minutes a day.
101	- Manual POPS overrides when MIPS feeds zeros for incomplete meters: Have the nightly MIPS-to-POPS feed mark incomplete meter volumes as incomplete instead of zero, so POPS keeps the Gas Control estimate.. Why: The fix was already being built when the problem surfaced (935.eml: the programmers were working on it that day), and the mail shows only one incident clearly caused by the zero feed, so the 2-per-month rate and the ongoing saving are not supported. Research that could settle it: Look for mail after March 2000 showing zeroed meters that MIPS still sent after the vendor fix (meters named, override requests to Volume Management), or a list of the affected meters (Tom Acton asked George Grant for one in 935.eml), to show the work continued and how often.
102	- Monthly industrial buyback/deficiency lists: Replace Kenneth Seaman's buyback list, Julie Meyers' spreadsheet and the hand-rebuilt Industrial report with one monthly report from Sitara deal tickets.. Why: The proposal counts the same list twice: Seaman's buyback list and the Industrial report are one stream of work, which Lloyd took over in February 2000. It counts 45 minutes a month for a report that 1253.eml says nobody had seen 'in a few months'. And it assumes a Sitara report could replace Meyers' spreadsheet, whose contents the mail never shows. Two earlier critics rejected this idea for these same reasons (decisions.md items 90 and 91), and this version answers none of them. Research that could settle it: Find what Meyers' 'UPDATED SPREADSHEET' attachments contain, and whether any of it is not already in Sitara buyback tickets (e.g. #148381). Find which months Lloyd actually produced the Industrial report after March 2000. Then estimate only the hand work a ticket report would really remove, likely 30-60 minutes a month.
103	- Month-end HPLC/ENA intercompany accrual variance list and chasing: A nightly tie-out report that compares the HPLC and ENA sides of every intercompany Sitara deal and emails schedulers any deal with a missing or mismatched side before the accrual runs.. Why: The mail shows the variance list only once, as a first-time request for a fix, and the other two cited messages are a one-off cleanup of an old 1999 deal and a one-time SAP cleanup with a deadline; the claim that the list is built by hand conflicts with mail saying an intercompany report already exists, and the work the proposal admits stays (researching each deal) is most of the cost. Research that could settle it: Look for Gregg Lenart variance lists or Thu Nguyen chase emails for other accrual months, and for how the intercompany or interdesk report is produced, to show the list is rebuilt by hand every month and how many deals are chased each time.
104	- Double scheduling and allocation of PG&E Texas (PGEV) transport under ENA plus an ENA/HPL desk-to-desk deal: Assign ENA's PGEV transport contracts to HPL so the gas is nominated, held and allocated under one contract with no desk-to-desk deal.. Why: The person who asked for this, Daren Farmer, decided against it a year later. In April 2001 (155.eml) he wrote that on PGEV 'we have been transporting the gas under ENA' and 'We want to keep these transport contracts with ENA', because HPL was being split off for AEP. The other cited mail is about different problems, and the daily and monthly minutes are guesses. Research that could settle it: Only new evidence would change this: mail after April 2001 showing that management decided to move the PGEV transport to HPL after all, or that the ENA leg and the desk-to-desk leg still had to be nominated and allocated by hand once HPL went to AEP.
105	- Monthly poll of risk leads for new book codes before NYMEX invoicing: A scheduled TAGG report, run before NYMEX invoicing, lists every book code that is new or held its first third-party financial deal that month, so settlements no longer has to poll the risk leads.. Why: The same work, from the same message (giron-d/sent/556.eml), is already saved as decision 13, 'Month-end poll of Risk for new book codes before NYMEX invoicing', which proposes the same automatic report.

So the 45 minutes counted for Seaman's list is the same work the proposal keeps as Lloyd's, and a critic has already rejected this idea for the same reason. Research that could settle it: Find what Julie Meyers' 'UPDATED SPREADSHEET' contains, whether Sitara tickets already hold buyback terms, and how many months Lloyd's report was actually produced. Then estimate only the one list that would really be removed.
- Houston Pipe Line Assignment, Termination & Expiration Report: Generate the report automatically from Global Contracts on the 15th and before bid week, sent to a self-service distribution group, instead of Cheryl Dudley compiling and emailing it by hand.. Why: The mail shows a monthly report (titled 03/01 and 04/01), not two a month: the 8 March issue was a one-time catch-up for the missed March report, and 2133.eml is the same message as 211.eml. Nothing shows the report is compiled by hand rather than printed from Global Contracts, and no list add or remove requests appear, so the 35 minutes saved per report has no support. The same idea has already been rejected twice in decisions.md for these reasons. Research that could settle it: Find mail showing how the report is produced (hand compilation or a Global Contracts printout) and how long it takes, more issues of the report to set the real frequency, and actual add or remove requests for the distribution list.
- Monthly Michcon Citygate ENA/Enron Canada out-of-balance: Re-book ENA deals 290657 and 290652 once to match Enron Canada's booking so the monthly ~$434 OA difference stops.. Why: This is a one-off fix to a single wrongly booked deal that the person doing the work had already asked for, not a change to how the work is done, and its savings depend on a deal term the mail never gives. Research that could settle it: Only a pattern would change this: several deals in the mail where ENA and Enron Canada book the same intercompany trade differently and settlements has to chase the desk each month, which would support a process change such as a booking check between the two entities.
- Monthly HPL Assignment, Termination, Expiration Report: Generate the report automatically from Global Contracts on a schedule and send it to a self-service subscription list instead of Contract Administration compiling and sending it by hand. Why: The mail never shows the report being compiled by hand. The only clue (1360.eml) is that Contract Administration already pulls such lists straight from Global Contracts, so the 45 minutes per issue and the 55 minutes a month saved are unsupported, and what is left (running a pull, attaching it, sending it to a saved list) takes only a few minutes. Research that could settle it: Find mail showing how the report is actually built (for example, retyping or checking contract entries by hand, or a revision caused by compiling errors, such as the February 2001 revision mentioned in 2114.eml) or naming the time it takes; without that, the savings stay at a few minutes a month.
- Daily email approval of the Enovate DPR: Automate the open-position tie-out and switch the three approvers to exception-only sign-off, with the final DPR released at a cutoff.. Why: The evidence is misread in places. 686.eml is not an approval, 221.eml shows an approver chasing the analyst rather than the analyst chasing approvals, and no reply from Tomaski or Radous is in the archive. The 10-minute daily saving is also too high: Giron's replies are mostly a one-word 'OK', and the approvers would still have to review the report. Research that could settle it: Look in the Tomaski, Radous, Falcone, Abel or Luong mailboxes (if any exist) for their own replies, for the analyst chasing missing approvals, and for how much work Giron's position tie-out takes. Then re-estimate the saving using only the reply and tie-out steps, which is likely 2 to 4 minutes a day.
- Manual POPS overrides when MIPS feeds zeros for incomplete meters: Have the nightly MIPS-to-POPS feed mark incomplete meter volumes as incomplete instead of zero, so POPS keeps the Gas Control estimate.. Why: The fix was already being built when the problem surfaced (935.eml: the programmers were working on it that day), and the mail shows only one incident clearly caused by the zero feed, so the 2-per-month rate and the ongoing saving are not supported. Research that could settle it: Look for mail after March 2000 showing zeroed meters that MIPS still sent after the vendor fix (meters named, override requests to Volume Management), or a list of the affected meters (Tom Acton asked George Grant for one in 935.eml), to show the work continued and how often.
- Monthly industrial buyback/deficiency lists: Replace Kenneth Seaman's buyback list, Julie Meyers' spreadsheet and the hand-rebuilt Industrial report with one monthly report from Sitara deal tickets.. Why: The proposal counts the same list twice: Seaman's buyback list and the Industrial report are one stream of work, which Lloyd took over in February 2000. It counts 45 minutes a month for a report that 1253.eml says nobody had seen 'in a few months'. And it assumes a Sitara report could replace Meyers' spreadsheet, whose contents the mail never shows. Two earlier critics rejected this idea for these same reasons (decisions.md items 90 and 91), and this version answers none of them. Research that could settle it: Find what Meyers' 'UPDATED SPREADSHEET' attachments contain, and whether any of it is not already in Sitara buyback tickets (e.g. #148381). Find which months Lloyd actually produced the Industrial report after March 2000. Then estimate only the hand work a ticket report would really remove, likely 30-60 minutes a month.
- Month-end HPLC/ENA intercompany accrual variance list and chasing: A nightly tie-out report that compares the HPLC and ENA sides of every intercompany Sitara deal and emails schedulers any deal with a missing or mismatched side before the accrual runs.. Why: The mail shows the variance list only once, as a first-time request for a fix, and the other two cited messages are a one-off cleanup of an old 1999 deal and a one-time SAP cleanup with a deadline; the claim that the list is built by hand conflicts with mail saying an intercompany report already exists, and the work the proposal admits stays (researching each deal) is most of the cost. Research that could settle it: Look for Gregg Lenart variance lists or Thu Nguyen chase emails for other accrual months, and for how the intercompany or interdesk report is produced, to show the list is rebuilt by hand every month and how many deals are chased each time.
- Double scheduling and allocation of PG&E Texas (PGEV) transport under ENA plus an ENA/HPL desk-to-desk deal: Assign ENA's PGEV transport contracts to HPL so the gas is nominated, held and allocated under one contract with no desk-to-desk deal.. Why: The person who asked for this, Daren Farmer, decided against it a year later. In April 2001 (155.eml) he wrote that on PGEV 'we have been transporting the gas under ENA' and 'We want to keep these transport contracts with ENA', because HPL was being split off for AEP. The other cited mail is about different problems, and the daily and monthly minutes are guesses. Research that could settle it: Only new evidence would change this: mail after April 2001 showing that management decided to move the PGEV transport to HPL after all, or that the ENA leg and the desk-to-desk leg still had to be nominated and allocated by hand once HPL went to AEP.
- Monthly poll of risk leads for new book codes before NYMEX invoicing: A scheduled TAGG report, run before NYMEX invoicing, lists every book code that is new or held its first third-party financial deal that month, so settlements no longer has to poll the risk leads.. Why: The same work, from the same message (giron-d/sent/556.eml), is already saved as decision 13, 'Month-end poll of Risk for new book codes before NYMEX invoicing', which proposes the same automatic report.

We have some new procedures for changing deals that affect other books.

cc:  
Subject: Changing Deals

Effective immediately,  if anyone changes any deal for any reason,  they need 
to provide a minibook with a before and after of exactly what they did.  This 
used to be a common courtesy,  but it looks like we need a stated policy in 
place.  You guys will therefore have to get minibook access to calc all books

for getting the appropriate people mini-book access as soon as possible.  It 
is critical that we get this done right away.  I know that this is not a 
one-sided issue.  No group is better or more important than any other group.  
It is therefore important that we do a better job of communicating across 
groups.

Thanks,

Jeff

136	 see it in the Path Manager either way. [Pinion, Richard]    To restate the=
137	 question for clarity, in path manager a scheduler pulls down a supply, mar=
138	ket and a service, adds any up/downstream contract information and/or Duns =
139	or DRN override and then saves it.  Unify looks for an old path with those =
140	exact variables and if it finds it re-uses it and if it does not find an ex=
141	act match creates a new path and path id.  I had been told that to do away =
142	with this function would create an unacceptably high amount of paths since =
143	any path once nominated on could not be deleted.  Has this changed???  At o=
144	ne time there were some schedulers that looked for the same path / activity=
145	 number match for nominations.  Texas Eastern was the only pipeline that ne=
146	eded the old activity numbers no matter how long it had been since they wer=
147	e used.  I spoke with Chris Ordway and the new LINK system no longer needs =
148	this to occur.  Transco uses activity numbers but uses the Activity number =
149	cross reference table to that function and therefore should not be affected=
150	.  Therefore, if it does not create a space or memory problem for Unify, I =
151	don't think that this constant old path look up is needed.   [Kinsey, Lisa]=
152	   Get rid of this. =20
153	
154	2)  The scheduling position window:  does anyone use this?  If not, we'll r=
155	emove the code logic that populates this window.  I have never seen a sched=
156	uler use this.  Please verify. [Pinion, Richard]   Originally such a window=
157	 was in use by everyone in the legacy system "Autonoms" so it was duplicate=
158	d in Unify by request.  It is not used in Unify now because of the other so=
159	phisticated tools Unify provides which obviate it's use.  The only value wo=
160	uld be notification of bridge errors or contract imbalances but there are o=
161	ther ways to determine those problems.  As voted on in a previous meeting o=
162	f the managers - Lose it!  [Kinsey, Lisa]  Why is this still here?=09=20
163	
164	3)  On the inventory pool list, does anyone need to see the Contarct Refere=
165	nces List?  Again, this code is called every retrieval time and doesn't app=
166	ear to be used from my observations.   If they do need this information, we=
167	 could provide it, but if not, I'd prefer to remove the functionality. [Pin=
168	ion, Richard]    This function is still very much in use by those with poin=
169	t based pipelines that must use the imbalance pool to facilitate balancing =
170	nomination volumes where multiple pipeline external pools exist and are pat=
171	hed through the same contract imbalance pool.  Keep it!  [Kinsey, Lisa]  Ye=
172	s.  We use this functionality a lot when pathing pools.=09=20
173	
174	4)  When pathing a one to many or many to one set of paths, what's the aver=
175	age number of paths they create at one time?  What about updates?  I know t=
176	hat ANR and NIGAS are big users of this feature since they have small packa=
177	ges of gas that they are limited in size to.  Does the system seem faster w=
178	hen you update one record at a time or chunks of records?  My real question=
179	 is how often they do this and for what number of paths on both Updates and=
180	 Inserts.  By update, I mean, going to the path list and changing an upstre=
181	am / downstream contract or a PSNA which in turn forces a new path to be cr=
182	eated. [Pinion, Richard]    This one to many or many to one pathing goes on=
183	 every day on every pipeline.  There is no 'average'.  They typically updat=
184	e a path with up/downstream meters or duns or dnb numbers one at a time how=
185	ever.  I hope this answers your question.  I see no change to this process =
186	at this time  [Kinsey, Lisa]  On some pipes this function is used more than=
187	 others.  When it is used we try and do as many paths as possible.  At this=
188	 time I do not see a need to change this process. =09=20
189	
190	5)  On brokered paths, do you want to utilize the same logic we have for Se=
191	rvice?  In other words, when updating Brokered arrangements, we don't incor=
192	porate the same logic for zeroing out the path and recreating a new arrangm=
193	ent link and hence sending it to be renominated?  Why do we do this for ser=
194	vice?  Is it because we have to renominate it?  I assume that's what it's f=
195	or since we don't send brokered paths to the pipe.  Anyway, with the Nomlog=
196	ic implmentation (two way interface), we were planning on having it behave =
197	the same way as service.  We need this verified. [Pinion, Richard]    We do=
198	n't perform the same logic for Brokered paths because these are not nominat=
199	ed to the pipeline and hence do not need a zero path to be resent to the pi=
200	peline when a significant change is made to the already nominated path.  I =
201	don't see a need to change the way Brokered paths are behaving at this time=
202	. [Kinsey, Lisa]  Agree with Richard.=09=20

Pat,

I have been working with Volume Management, Settlements, Vance, and Bob to 
clean up some prior period and prior-to-current month issues.  This process 
should result in a correction to booked profit/loss for Vance and the desk.  
This has brought to my attention that we have been paying some parties 
manually for volumes when deals are not correctly entered.  I would propose 
that Logistics be included in the communication of when checks are manually 
cut.  It would be especially beneficial if we tracked manual checks by 
counterparty, meter, and/or deal ticket id or price.  I feel that this will 
allow us to spot and resolve potential issues more effectively.

Please let me know what your thoughts are on this matter.  

Thank you for your time,

Mary
